the-2002-cia-world-factbook: Every year the Central Intelligence Agency publishes this thick reference volume profiling nearly every country on earth. Each entry packs in geography, population, government, economy, and military facts in compact tables and short notes. Researchers, students, and the simply curious have long used the Factbook as a quick, reliable snapshot of the world as it stood in 2002.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-meadow-brook: Laura Lee Hope takes Nan, Bert, Freddie, and Flossie Bobbsey to the country in this cheerful series installment. At Meadow Brook the twins enjoy farm fun, new friends, and a mild mystery to solve. Generations of young readers grew up with the Bobbseys, whose wholesome adventures made them among the most beloved children in American books.
favorite-dishes-a-columbian-autograph-so: Compiled for the 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago, this souvenir cookbook gathers favorite recipes contributed — and autographed — by famous women of the day. Beyond its practical dishes, the book is a social document of the fair that introduced America to the modern world. A tasty piece of history.
the-grey-fairy-book: Andrew Lang's Grey Fairy Book gathers thirty-five tales from around the world — French, German, Italian, and more exotic sources. Princes, giants, and clever youngest sons populate stories chosen for their strangeness and charm. Part of Lang's beloved rainbow of fairy books, it has delighted children for over a century.
miss-parloa-s-new-cook-book: Maria Parloa — America's first celebrity cooking teacher — offers hundreds of tested recipes in this comprehensive guide. From soups to desserts, her clear instructions brought professional standards to home kitchens. A landmark of American cookery and a fascinating record of what the nation ate.
the-belgian-cookbook: Compiled for wartime relief, this Belgian cookbook offers the hearty dishes of little Belgium — stews, mussels, and Flemish favorites. Its sale aided refugees of the Great War. Good food for a good cause. Waterzooi, carbonnades, and waffles share these pages, each recipe a small act of mercy.
the-green-fairy-book: Andrew Lang's Green Fairy Book gathers tales from many lands — Spanish, Chinese, and more — in his beloved colored series. Magic, wit, and wonder fill its pages. A childhood treasure for over a century. Dragons, fairies, and clever youngest sons await within its covers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domesday-book: A 1913 entry on Domesday Book — the Conqueror's great survey. Herbert Thurston unfolds its famous pages. The commissioners wrote the land's tale. The Exchequer keeps the vellum treasure. The record of the Norman England. Its Little Domesday is famed.

the-blue-fairy-book: Andrew Lang's Blue Fairy Book (1889) collects classic fairy tales beautifully illustrated. Cinderella and Beauty appear in these pages. The Tower library holds the full complete text. It enchanted Victorian nurseries everywhere happily. The colored fairy books became beloved classics. Children met magic through these wonderful pages. The collection endures through generations.
govdocs-archive_org-mazdean-critique-of-:
The Shkand-Gumanig Vizar, the Doubt-Dispelling Exposition, is a ninth-century Zoroastrian defense of the faith written by Mardanfarrokh, son of Hurmazddad. He wrote in Persia, in a land already ruled by Islam for two centuries, to answer doubts among his fellow Zoroastrians.

The work reasons through God's goodness, the origin of evil, and the claims of rival faiths, including a direct critique of Islam. It is one of the richest surviving works of Zoroastrian theology. One caution: the text in this copy is corrupted by a character-encoding shift, which garbles the reading in places.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CookBook_Cook_B: A promotional flyer from the Delmarva Poultry Industry, Inc. announces the finals of the National Chicken Cooking Contest. The sheet was made to publicize the contest's final round, in which home cooks competed with chicken dishes. Nothing in the surviving record gives the flyer's date or names the finalists, so it stands mainly as a piece of poultry industry publicity from the contest era.
govdocs-archive_org-phantom-gerhard-haup:
Gerhart Hauptmann won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and his 1922 novel Phantom shows his darker side at full strength. Bayard Quincy Morgan translated it into English. The story follows a minor clerk who becomes obsessed with a strange young woman he barely knows.

Hauptmann mixes crime, longing, and mirage as the clerk's fixation pulls his whole life apart, page by page. The novel reads partly as confession and partly as fever dream. It stands as a German classic of the years after the First World War, when many writers were drawn to minds coming loose from ordinary life.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Bolton_B:
John Bolton, Donald Trump's former national security adviser, wrote a memoir called The Room Where It Happened. In June 2020 the Trump administration went to court to try to stop it. A National Security Archive posting from June 19, 2020 covers that fight and places it in a longer line of cases over officials publishing what the government calls classified secrets.

The posting includes documentation of earlier prepublication review cases, the system under which former officials must clear manuscripts before printing. That history is the Archive's contribution: book fights look new each time, but the review machinery is old and its rules shape what the public learns. Readers get both the breaking story of one famous memoir and the background needed to judge the censorship claim behind it.
podcast-dannyjones-uQPAVic3Jok:
Researcher Carl Hayden Smith joins Danny Jones to tell how he was injected with DMT so teams could study the fabric of reality. Smith works on how tech and drugs shift the sense of self. He speaks as a test subject here.

Smith tells what the drug showed him, step by step, under lab watch. He talks about the beings, the sense of a built world, and what stayed with him after. Jones asks how a lab can use such wild reports as data. Listeners get a rare first hand lab tale. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his account.
podcast-joerogan-zv8pjyJH4Ok:
Dr. Gabor Mate talks trauma and healing with Joe Rogan in episode 1869 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mate, a Canadian physician, argues that addiction and many illnesses grow out of early wounds. His book The Myth of Normal questions what modern life does to body and mind.

Mate explains his method of compassionate inquiry, asking patients what happened to them rather than what is wrong with them. He shares stories from his work with addicts in Vancouver's hardest streets. Rogan asks about his own habits and stresses under that lens. The talk offers a gentle, searching view of pain and recovery.
podcast-tuckercarlson-HzHSK7WXqok:
A Gold Star father joins Tucker Carlson to accuse the Biden team of shameful conduct. His son died in service, and grief fuels every word. His quote gives the episode its title: we were used.

He describes the return of the fallen and the words of officials. He says leaders staged honor while dodging blame for a failed exit. Carlson lets the father's anger run without softening it. The episode honors the dead through a parent's charge. It will hit hardest with military families who feel their loss was mishandled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-przemysl-samb: Przemyśl, Sambor, and Sanok were the dioceses of Galicia's Ruthenians. This entry covers their bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith of the Ukrainian highlands: their wooden cathedrals crown the Carpathian hills in living faith and song and prayer.
the-red-fairy-book: The second of Andrew Lang's famous colored fairy books, gathering thirty-seven traditional tales from France, Germany, Russia, Romania, and beyond. Princes, witches, giants, and clever youngest sons fill its pages, each story retold in Lang's clear Victorian English. Like the Blue Fairy Book before it, the volume helped shape what English-speaking children imagine when they hear the words "fairy tale."
the-1995-cia-world-factbook: The U.S. Central Intelligence Agency's 1995 country-by-country reference, the same public almanac it still publishes today. Every nation gets a compact profile: geography, population, government, economy, military, and communications, frozen as of the mid-1990s. For researchers and the curious, it is a snapshot of the world just after the Cold War, when new countries were still appearing on the map.
the-violet-fairy-book: Andrew Lang's violet volume gathers fairy tales from the Balkans, Scandinavia, and other corners of Europe less familiar to English readers. Dragons, clever peasants, and enchanted princesses populate stories chosen for their freshness, many appearing in English for the first time. Like all the colored fairy books, it is storytelling treasure, retold with Lang's easy grace.
the-yellow-fairy-book: The yellow entry in Andrew Lang's rainbow of fairy-tale collections, drawing on German, French, and Russian sources. Its stories of talking animals, wicked stepmothers, and brave youngest children are told in the clear, unhurried style that made the series famous. For young readers it is pure magic; for adults, a window into the folk imagination of old Europe.
flying-machines-construction-and-operati: William Jackman's 1910 practical guide to airplanes: how they are built, how they fly, and how to operate one. Written when aviation was a daring new craft, it explains engines, controls, and airframes for the enthusiastic beginner. A fascinating technical snapshot from the heroic age of flight.
the-1997-cia-world-factbook: The CIA's 1997 country-by-country almanac: every nation's geography, people, government, and economy as of the late 1990s. A snapshot of the world between the Cold War and the internet age. The public reference, frozen in time.
the-1998-cia-world-factbook: The CIA's 1998 almanac of every country: geography, people, government, and economy, compiled by American intelligence. Fascinating as a snapshot of the world at century's end. A treasure trove of facts and figures. Historians mine it for the state of the world just before the new millennium.
the-crimson-fairy-book: Andrew Lang’s Crimson Fairy Book: more fairy tales from around the world, in his famous colored series. Enchanting stories for children, beautifully told, the magic continuing. Every child should own the whole rainbow set.
the-lilac-fairy-book: Andrew Lang's Lilac Fairy Book: the twelfth fairy book. Tales from many lands. The beloved series continues. Childhood's treasury, lang's twelfth fairy book, tales from many lands, childhood's treasury, Lang, fairy, Andrew Lang, twelfth, treasury.
the-2000-cia-world-factbook: The 2000 CIA World Factbook profiles every nation on earth. Geography, people, government, and economy appear in compact entries. The handy reference serves students and travelers alike. A clear snapshot of the world at century's end.
nasa-tm-19660025355-failure-information-: Every failure teaches something — if someone writes it down. This 1966 NASA failure information notebook compiles failure reports and lessons learned. The collection gave engineers a reference for what went wrong and how to avoid repeating it.
doe-osti-2588955-infrared-thermometer-in: Point-and-shoot heat readers got their DOE handbook, and this manual covers the infrared guns. The pages walk through the how-to. The techs get their reference. The guns were infrared. The how-to was walked. The reference was tech.
doe-osti-2997625-efficiency-project-play: Efficiency projects got their playbook, and this DOE text lays out the project approach. The pages detail the methods. The energy managers get their guide. The projects were efficiency. The approach was project. The managers got guides. The approach was detailed.
doe-osti-3376012-cyber-informed-engineer: CIE got workbook-EoT/HoT'd, and this DOE workbook covers train communications. The pages detail the end findings. The security folks get their data. The engineering was cyber-informed. The data were security. The HoT were EoT. The communications were train.
doe-osti-3630799-power-lane-county-elect: Power Lane County got grid-handbooked, and this DOE handbook covers electric grids. The pages detail the power findings. The grid folks get their data. The handbook was county. The data were grid. The Lane were Power. The electric were grid.
a-pr-mvad-szok: A prémvadászok, the Hungarian translation of a Verne tale. Verne in Hungarian. This book preserves that translation. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.
the-blue-jar-story-book: The Blue Jar Story Book, Maria Edgeworth's tales. The jar's stories. This book preserves that children's book. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
20830-the-good-housekeeping-marriage-boo:
California students asked for a course in marriage relations, and a New York paper took note. The Good Housekeeping Marriage Book, from 1938, grew from that fresh demand. Its pages gather counsel from men and women who wrote on married life.

Courtship, money, sex, in-laws, and children all get frank, plain treatment. Good Housekeeping lent its trusted name to guide young couples of the day. The book marks a shift toward open, expert talk on marriage. Readers can see what counted as wise counsel on the eve of the Second World War, in middle-class American terms.
20952-a-jolly-jingle-book:
A little red man in a little red house with ivory gates stars in A Jolly Jingle-Book. He will talk and laugh at all you do, the riddle rhyme warns. Luther H. Cary's 1913 book of jingles dares children to name that red man.

Rhymes, riddles, and tongue play fill the book for young readers at home. Its verses beg to be read aloud, chanted, and guessed at in turns. Such jingle books fed the nursery trade in cheerful, harmless fun. The red man, your own tongue, gives the game away to sharp children, who then delight in springing it on others.
21007-the-bird-study-book:
Birds and spring feel like one word, says T. Gilbert Pearson in The Bird Study Book. Wild song, flashing wings, and mad dashes through thickets all spring from mating fire. His 1917 book opens on that riot of the breeding season.

Pearson, a founder of the Audubon movement, teaches how to watch birds with care. Nests, migration, food, and protection fill his plain, keen chapters. He urges readers to guard birds, not just name them on lists. The book helped turn bird study into a mass American pastime, binoculars in hand and notebook ready at dawn.
19879-five-pebbles-from-the-brook:
Five Pebbles from the Brook examines the grounds of Christianity. Its subtitle states the method: comparing the New Testament with the Old. The author pictures scripture as an edifice on a foundation. The Law and the Prophets are that foundation, he argues. If the later books irreconcilably clash with the older revelation, their authority falls. The argument proceeds text against text, closely.

George Bethune English wrote this attack in the early republic. He had traveled in Egypt and served in its army. His pebbles are five arguments slung at orthodoxy, David-style. Deist and freethinking pamphlets like his stirred American pulpits. The book survives as evidence of that fight. It is combative, learned, and unmistakably of 1813.
20652-ring-o-roses-a-nursery-rhyme-pictu:
L. Leslie Brooke illustrated Ring o' Roses, a nursery rhyme picture book, with pictures in color and in black and white. Brooke's drawings for children's classics were among the best of their age. The rhymes here are the first poems of the nursery.

Here is the finger rhyme every child learns. This little pig went to market, this little pig stayed at home, and this little pig had roast beef. This little pig had none, and the last cried wee, wee, wee, all the way home. Brooke's pigs act out the rhyme with comic charm.
21469-the-mate-of-the-lily-or-notes-from:
Harry Musgrave ships as an apprentice officer in W. H. G. Kingston's The Mate of the Lily. His father, Captain Musgrave, never came home from his last voyage, leaving his mother near destitute. Her brother Jack, mate of the Lily, steps in to support the family.

The Lily seeks a return cargo in the Java seas, where clues point to the lost captain. Storms, a volcano, grounding, and pirate attacks block the search. Near the end they find the captain alive, though sunk in despair. News of home revives him, and suspense holds the tale tight to the last.
21574-the-poacher-or-joseph-rushbrook:
Joseph Rushbrook's tale opens on a blustering November night in 1812 in Captain Marryat's The Poacher. Three men reel out of an alehouse, two half-carrying the third between them. Chapter one, Marryat warns, holds more ale than argument.

Rushbrook's poaching sets him against keepers, law, and his own better hopes. The book, Marryat's eighteenth, appeared in 1841 after his great sea tales. Village life, crime, and conscience get equal weight in the telling. Marryat knew the world of game laws from the inside, and his poacher is no stage villain but a full, flawed man.
21874-the-bay-and-padie-book:
Australian children sing through this 1917 book of kiddie songs by Furnley Maurice, with pictures by Vera Hamilton and Cyril Dobbs. Bay and Padie are small boys whose world holds trains, trams, sparrows, ponies, and grubs. The Shadow Show lists the wonders: aeroplanes, paper darts, woodmen's carts, and barking pups that knock the postman off his bike. Oh, what a lot of lots of things for little boys to see, the chorus runs.

Maurice thanks Sydney papers for leave to reprint pieces like Kitchen Lullaby and Little Boys. The book ran to a second edition within months, wholly printed in Australia. Its slang and sunshine are pure period Australia. Grown readers will find their grandparents' nursery world preserved in rhyme.
21914-the-woggle-bug-book:
Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., takes a walk down an American main street in L. Frank Baum's Woggle-Bug Book of 1905. The initials mean Highly Magnified and Thoroughly Educated, titles earned in the Land of Oz. Separated from his Oz companions, the giant insect has four hands and time hanging heavy on all of them. He marches with an air of importance, proud of his learning.

Ike Morgan's pictures show the Bug's queer figure, which he himself never suspects. In America his Oz education proves less remarkable than he hopes. Baum builds the joke gently: vanity in a frock coat, six feet of it. The book is a short, sunny offshoot of the Oz tales, made for readers who wanted one more visit with its oddest scholar.
21935-prince-prigio-from-his-own-fairy-b:
Prince Prigio of Pantouflia is too clever for his own good in Andrew Lang's fairy tale from his own invented book. Lang confesses in his preface that the famous colored Fairy Books were gathered from old tales, not made up by him. This one he did invent, with help from Pantouflia's historical papers. Pantouflia's kings descend from a Greek family that dodged the Crusades. Their crest is a dormouse asleep on a green field.

Prigio, blessed or cursed with magic gifts and a too-logical mind, must learn what cleverness cannot do. Lang writes the tale as a sly lesson in the limits of cleverness, dressed as pure fun. Pantouflia later got a second visit in Prince Ricardo. The humor still sparkles for grown readers as much as children.
22197-the-goody-naughty-book:
Sarah Cory Rippey wrote The Goody-Naughty Book in 1913 to teach small children their manners through stories. Its full title promises the goody side and the naughty side of child life. In one tale, little Rose-Red is comforted in her mother's arms after a quarrel. Ruthie is probably sorry now, her mother says, and Rose-Red must be ready to forgive when the apology comes.

Each short story pairs a fault with its gentle cure. Table manners, temper, truthfulness, and kindness all take their turn. The language is simple and the morals are spoken aloud by mothers. Such books lined the nursery shelves of progressive homes before child psychology changed the fashion.
22231-peak-and-prairie-from-a-colorado-s:
Anna Fuller gathered Peak and Prairie from a Colorado sketch-book in 1894. Fuller warns that her sketches are little more than hints caught by a single observer. Her field is narrow, but she promises it offers unusual variety. The health resort she calls Springtown stands at the centre, drawing many kinds of people into one small place.

Invalids, miners, tourists, and ranch folk cross in her sketches. Pike's Peak country gave Fuller her material, as it did in her earlier novel. She writes with humour and a traveller's quick sympathy. The book belongs to the local-colour movement that mapped America's regions for eastern readers, and Colorado Springs lives in it.
22335-harrison-s-new-nursery-picture-boo:
Harrison's New Nursery Picture Book offered children pictures and short pieces in one volume. Its list of plates shows what young readers were shown. Robinson Crusoe appears again and again in the illustrations.

Crusoe is cast on an uninhabited island in one picture. In others he finds a footprint and fires at attackers. Friday stands beside him in another plate. Other pictures show Edwin on his new rocking-horse and May-day amusements. A visit to an Indian juggler adds exotic flavor. Picture books like this shaped early reading. They mixed adventure, morals, and play in pages made to be looked at first.
22495-the-new-pun-book:
The New Pun Book, copyrighted in 1906 by Carey-Stafford, collects jokes built on wordplay. Each entry is a short exchange ending in a pun. The humor is quick, mild, and made for reading aloud.

He's a professional grafter, one joke announces of a nurseryman. Another asks what Fatty Schultz the butcher weighs: meat. A hardware sign reading cast iron sinks draws a knowing nod. Everyone, the joker says, is already wise to that fact. How are you today gets the answer, oh, I can't kick. Joke books like this filled railway journeys and parlor evenings. Readers get Edwardian humor in its lightest, groaning form.
